title: Cumbria's most haunted places revealed in new book Spooky Britain
excerpt: Explore Cumbria’s most haunted places, from Muncaster Castle and Furness Abbey to Aira Force, in Peter Naldrett’s Spooky Britain guide to ghost stories.
content:
Having spent two years researching the most haunted and eerie places in Britain, the author of Spooky Britain reveals why Cumbria is one of the most chilling of counties

There’s something about a good ghost story that makes people sit up and pay attention, even if they’re not normally a believer in paranormal activity.

Stories about spectres dwelling in famous buildings, monsters roaming in local woods and strange sightings in the skies, are all captivating tales to give these darkening nights an air of excited mystery.

I’ve journeyed the nation to discover which places will offer the best experience for those into gruesome history and spooky goings on. The results have gone into a book called Spooky Britain, a companion to hauntings and weird episodes from the past that refuse to disappear.

While you might expect historic cities like York, London and Edinburgh to house more than their fair share of spirits, I was amazed to discover the rich ghostly heritage of Cumbria.

There are many pubs, walks, old buildings and lakes in the county where I would make sure I travelled to with a good friend and certainly wouldn’t be tempted to venture on a misty evening with a full moon in the sky.

There are so many Cumbrian spooky hotspots that they wouldn’t all fit into the 100 chapters I had available in Spooky Britain.

So, let’s go on a Halloween journey around Cumbria to see where your best chances of spotting a Lakeland spectre are.

Muncaster Castle (Image: Paul Hudson)

A great place to start is Muncaster Castle, near Ravenglass. Sightings of ghosts have been reported here for decades, and the castle has been the focus of many paranormal investigations.

Some reckon it’s among the most haunted buildings in the country, with spectral residents including Tom Fool, Maggie the Crying Child, the Lady in White and a spirit dressed in black.

Much of the activity tends to focus on the Tapestry Room, where a visit in the daytime can be freaky enough. But imagine if you got to spend all night within the ghostly four walls.

Well, that potentially disturbing experience is available to those with steady nerves thanks to the castle’s ‘Ghost Sit’ experience. This allows you and a group of your friends to spend the night in the notorious Tapestry Room if you have the backbone for it.

Furness (Image: Geneve Bartholomew-Brand)

Let’s remain in south Lakeland and spend some time at Furness Abbey. These are fabulously atmospheric ruins, occupied by monks before the dissolution of the monasteries. If the stories are true, several of the monks have not left and spend the afterlife trapped around these ancient stones.

One of the most famous hauntings of the abbey is by a headless monk, seen in the area passing through on horseback. Another monk, with head still attached, has been known to hang out on an abbey staircase. When you factor in the rumours about treasure, tunnels and holy relics beneath the site, it becomes a very intriguing place to be.

If you’re still on the lookout for ghosts in southern Cumbria, call in at Levens Hall, near Kendal. You might catch a glimpse of a Grey Lady there, and perhaps even a sighting of a ghost dog that has been seen bounding around the place.

Cursing Stone (Image: Les Haines)

Another ancient building with a spooky history is Carlisle Castle, which is said to be haunted by several apparitions, including a Scottish lady bricked up inside the castle walls. And while you’re in the city centre, why not visit the Cursing Stone? It’s a piece of public artwork engraved with an old curse that was put on a family with a bad reputation, and has been a controversial addition to the city. Some have blamed it for local flooding, and even the challenging times experienced by Carlisle United!

Let’s head into the National Park now, and to Aira Force waterfall, at Ullswater. The ghost of a girl called Emma is said to spend melancholy evenings here, a troubled spirit from medieval times. Emma was engaged to a knight called Sir Eglamore who went off on the Crusades. It left her so sorrowful she started to sleepwalk to Aira Force, tumbling in and drowning on one tragic night. The tale was addressed by Wordsworth in his poem The Somnambulist, and therefore passed down the generations.

When in need of refreshment, the Kirkstone Pass Inn is always a good place to head. Sitting outside on a fine day brings rewarding views but find yourself at the top of this famous pass on a bleak, misty day and it will provide a very different vibe. It’s very easy to believe the haunted stories that accompany this 15th century watering hole when visibility is down to zero and you hear whispers on the wind. Are the tales of a dead coaching boy true? What about those of a woman found hanged nearby and the former worker blamed for poltergeist activity? Keep an eye on your pint when you’re there, just in case.

When I was hiking the fells around 20 years ago, our group froze in its tracks as we saw a large black animal around 200 metres ahead of us effortlessly jump over a dry stone wall. Some wanted to turn back, but we pressed on after waiting long enough for it to have left the area.

There was nobody else about to claim ownership of a dog, and besides, the leap it made was not very ‘dog like.’ So, was this the much talked about Beast of Cumbria, a black panther-like creature that has had sightings reported in the national press?

This county is indeed an intense centre of all kinds of strange and mysterious goings-on. Maybe you’ve experienced something unusual yourself? If so, please get in touch because I’d love to hear about it. And if you’re still a sceptic, try to keep an open mind. You never know what’s waiting for you around the corner…

Spooky Britain by Peter Naldrett is available now through Bloomsbury.
